title: The Fool's Speech: False Apostles and Paul's Sufferings
summary: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a little foolishness as he, jealous for them like a father who has promised his daughter in marriage, fears they are being led astray by those who preach another Jesus. He defends his refusal to accept their financial support and exposes his rivals as false apostles disguised as servants of righteousness, as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. Then, speaking deliberately as a fool, he boasts, but his boast is a catalogue of beatings, dangers, hunger, and anxiety for the churches, ending with an undignified escape over the wall of Damascus.
story: Chapter 10 set out the terms of Paul's conflict with his critics in Corinth. In chapter 11 the conflict comes into the open. Paul names his rivals' claims and answers them, and then begins what is usually called the fool's speech (11:16-12:10), in which he reluctantly adopts their habit of self-praise in order to show how empty it is. The speech reaches its climax in chapter 12, with the vision of paradise and the thorn in the flesh.
historical:
The hardships Paul lists in verses 23-27 are important evidence for his life, and many are not recorded in Acts. Acts mentions one beating with rods, at Philippi (Acts 16:22-23), and one stoning, at Lystra (Acts 14:19); Paul says he was beaten with rods three times. The forty lashes minus one were a synagogue punishment based on Deuteronomy 25:3, which limited a beating to forty strokes; the practice of stopping at thirty-nine guarded against exceeding the limit by miscounting. That Paul received this five times shows he kept attending synagogues and submitting to their discipline. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. None of the three shipwrecks is the one in Acts 27, which happened later.

Verses 32-33 refer to Aretas IV, king of the Nabataean Arabs, who ruled from about 9 BC to about AD 40 from his capital at Petra. His governor, or ethnarch, in Damascus tried to arrest Paul soon after his conversion. Acts 9:23-25 tells the same escape, attributing the plot to Jews in Damascus; both may have been involved. How Aretas's official came to have such power in Damascus is debated, since the city was generally under Roman control, but the episode fits the late 30s AD.
cultural:
Paul pictures himself in verse 2 as the father of a bride. In Jewish custom a betrothal was a binding commitment, and the father was responsible to present his daughter as a virgin to her husband at the wedding. Israel was often pictured in the Old Testament as God's bride (Hosea 2:19-20; Isaiah 54:5), and Paul applies the image to the church and Christ.

Paul's refusal of money from Corinth made sense in a culture shaped by patronage. To accept support from a wealthy member would make Paul that person's client, obligated to him and seen as belonging to his household. It would also place him among the many travelling teachers who lived off their hearers. The Corinthians, or some of them, seem to have taken his refusal as an insult or as a sign that he was not a real apostle. Paul instead accepted help from the Macedonian churches (verse 9; Philippians 4:15-16). Self-praise was a recognized part of Greek rhetoric, but it was also widely criticized as vulgar; Paul's fool's speech plays on that tension, parodying the boasting of his rivals by boasting in his humiliations.
literary: The chapter is saturated with irony. Paul calls his own speech foolishness and insists he speaks "as a fool" (verses 16-17, 21), a device that lets him say what he could not say straightforwardly. The rivals are ironically called "super-apostles" (verse 5). The list of hardships (verses 23-29) takes the form of a boast of achievements but reverses its content: instead of victories, honors, and eloquence, he lists beatings, dangers, and sleepless nights. The eightfold repetition of the Greek word for danger in verse 26 creates a relentless rhythm. The climax is deliberately anticlimactic. Where a Roman soldier might boast of being first over an enemy wall, Paul's most memorable exploit is being lowered down a wall in a basket to run away.

outline.t: A godly jealousy: another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel
Why Paul preached free of charge
False apostles disguised as servants of righteousness
Boasting in labors, dangers, and daily concern for the churches
Boasting in weakness: the escape from Damascus

doctrines.note: Paul's "daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches" (verse 28) is the heaviest burden in his list. The church is Christ's bride, to be kept pure in her devotion, and pastoral care means feeling the weakness and stumbling of others as one's own (verse 29).

Paul presents suffering, not success, as the mark of a true servant of Christ. The list is not a complaint but evidence: his life takes the shape of the crucified Lord he serves. He boasts "of the things that show my weakness" (verse 30).

Paul warns against "a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed" and "a different gospel" (verse 4). There is a truth about Jesus that can be distorted, and false teaching can come with impressive credentials and the look of righteousness, just as Satan "masquerades as an angel of light".

words.note: Zelos, zeal or jealousy. It can describe destructive envy, but it can also describe God's jealous love for his people, which refuses to share them with rivals (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). Paul's "godly jealousy" is protective love like God's own.

Pseudapostolos, false apostle, found only here in the New Testament and possibly coined by Paul. The problem was not that these teachers lacked gifts or credentials but that they served a different Jesus and exploited the church.

Metaschematizo, to change outward form, to disguise, to masquerade. It appears three times in verses 13-15, of the false apostles, of Satan, and of his servants. The word stresses outward appearance that does not match inner reality.

Aphrosyne, foolishness, senselessness. Paul uses it of his own boasting (verses 1, 17, 21). By calling his boast folly, he signals that the whole contest of self-praise belongs to a way of thinking the gospel overturns.

christ: Paul's concern is for the Corinthians' "simple and pure devotion to Christ" (verse 3), pictured as a bride's loyalty to her husband. The danger is "a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed" (verse 4): it matters who Jesus is. The list of sufferings shows what it looks like to follow a crucified Lord. Paul does not claim that his sufferings save anyone, but his life reproduces the pattern of Christ's, who was also beaten, despised, and counted weak. When he chooses to boast in weakness (verse 30), he is preparing for the revelation of chapter 12, where Christ's power is perfected in weakness, and for the confession of 13:4 that Christ "was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power".

hard.q: Who were the "super-apostles", and is Paul being unfair to his rivals?
hard.a:
Paul never names them, and scholars have long debated their identity. One older view, associated with the nineteenth-century Tübingen school of F. C. Baur, linked the super-apostles with the leading apostles in Jerusalem (Peter, James, and John), and saw the letter as evidence of deep conflict between Paul and Jerusalem. A more moderate form of that view, argued by C. K. Barrett among others, holds that the super-apostles were the Jerusalem leaders whose names the intruders invoked, while the false apostles of verse 13 were the intruders themselves. Most scholars today distinguish them from the Jerusalem leaders: Paul speaks respectfully of those leaders elsewhere (Galatians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:5-11), while the super-apostles of chapter 11 appear to be the same intruders he calls false apostles in verse 13. Some think they claimed to represent Jerusalem without its approval.

As for fairness, Paul's language is fierce, and we hear only his side. But his charges are specific: the rivals preach a different Jesus, commend themselves, exploit the church (verse 20), and boast in credentials rather than in Christ. He does not attack them for their ethnicity, which he shares (verse 22), or for accepting support as such, since he defends the right of apostles to receive it (1 Corinthians 9:4-14). His target is a way of ministry that serves the minister rather than Christ.

questions: Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray from simple and pure devotion to Christ. What forces in your life most pull you away from that simple devotion?
Paul boasts in his weaknesses rather than his achievements. What would it look like for a church or leader today to do the same?
Paul says he feels daily pressure over all the churches, and burns with grief when others are led into sin. Whose weakness do you carry as your own?
